claims.text: The target material is a multiphase eutectic HEA containing an FCC matrix and a sigma phase.
The target material has a refined microstructure.
The distinct phases have different oxidation rates at elevated temperature.
Differential oxidation at FCC-sigma boundaries produces non-uniform, mechanically weak oxide films.
Mechanical wear ruptures oxide films on the HEA surface.
Oxide-film rupture exposes fresh metal.
Oxide-film rupture promotes adhesive and abrasive wear.
A potential difference between FCC and sigma phases causes galvanic corrosion.
Galvanic corrosion localizes at sigma-phase interfaces and phase boundaries.
Repeated film rupture and localized galvanic corrosion form a feedback loop that raises degradation beyond the sum of isolated wear and corrosion.
The proposed coupled test uses a 3.5 wt.% NaCl electrolyte at approximately 300 degrees Celsius.
Oxygen partial pressure and chloride content are controlled during testing.
The microstructure must remain stable without phase transformations during the test.
Wear-only and corrosion-only tests under matched high-temperature conditions provide the isolated baselines.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce significantly greater total degradation than either isolated exposure.
Coupled exposure will increase abrasive wear through intermittent oxide-film rupture.
Coupled exposure will enhance corrosion rates at phase boundaries through localized galvanic cells.
Coupled exposure will produce more severe wear tracks and higher pit densities.
The magnitude of the coupled enhancement is sensitive to oxygen partial pressure, chloride concentration, and phase composition.
Homogenizing the interfacial oxidation response by microalloying or heat treatment should reduce the synergistic degradation.

contradictions.description: The mechanism defines synergy as combined degradation exceeding the sum of isolated wear and corrosion. The falsification rule first describes failure of interfacial modification to reduce synergy, but then equates that condition with combined degradation being comparable to the isolated sum. Comparability to the sum indicates absence or removal of synergy, not persistence of unreduced synergy.
